def test_msix_mem_restore_no_ur(sd, logger):
    """
    Verify the kernel restores MSI-X messages with memory decoding enabled:
    FLR a vfio-bound ConnectX PF whose saved config has COMMAND.Memory
    cleared and check that the MSI-X-table restore does not fault as an
    Unsupported Request / RP PIO error / DPC containment.

    The fix is NOT yet upstream: a FAIL is remediated by backporting
    "PCI/MSI: Enable memory decoding before restoring MSI-X messages"
    (patch 4/4 of the v20 "Error recovery for vfio-pci devices on s390x"
    series).

    DESTRUCTIVE: on an unpatched kernel this wedges the target NIC and a BMC
    power cycle may be required to recover it.

    JIRA: DGX-17078
    PATCH: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260622171840.1618-5-alifm@linux.ibm.com/
    """
    target_bdf_env = "GLT_MSIX_MEM_RESTORE_BDF"
    pci_command_offset = "0x04"
    pci_command_memory = 0x2
    # Kernel-log fragments that identify the UR / RP PIO / DPC / AER signature
    # of the unpatched MSI-X restore path. Each is checked for as a substring
    # of the post-FLR kernel log window via glt_utils.get_kernel_log().
    fault_signatures = (
        "DPC: containment event",
        "RP PIO",
        "Memory Request received UR Completion",
        "AER: Uncorrected",
        "severity=Uncorrected",
    )
    patch_fail_msg = (
        "MSI-X restore raised an Unsupported Request / DPC containment — kernel "
        "lacks the memory-decoding fix. Consider backporting "
        "https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260622171840.1618-5-alifm@linux.ibm.com/ "
        "(PCI/MSI: Enable memory decoding before restoring MSI-X messages) to "
        "fix it."
    )
    msix_bdf_re = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-f]{4}:[0-9a-f]{2}:[0-9a-f]{2}\.[0-7]$")

    if (not glt_utils.is_cli_available("lspci")
            or not glt_utils.is_cli_available("setpci")):
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("lspci/setpci not available; install pciutils")

    bdf = os.environ.get(target_bdf_env, "").strip().lower()
    if not bdf:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(
            f"set {target_bdf_env} to an expendable ConnectX BDF; this test "
            "is destructive and may require a BMC power cycle to recover")
    dev_path = f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}"
    if not msix_bdf_re.match(bdf) or not os.path.exists(dev_path):
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(f"configured device {bdf} not present")

    safe, reason = _resolve_and_validate_target(bdf)
    if not safe:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(reason)

    try:
        iommu_groups = os.listdir("/sys/kernel/iommu_groups")
    except OSError:
        iommu_groups = []
    if not iommu_groups:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("IOMMU not enabled; vfio requires IOMMU")

    if not glt_utils.is_cli_available("vfio_mlx5"):
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("vfio_mlx5 not found; install DOCA libvfio-mlx5")

    try:
        subprocess.run(["modprobe", "vfio-pci"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("vfio-pci module unavailable")

    drv_link = f"{dev_path}/driver"

    sd.progress_record_time(test_msix_mem_restore_no_ur.__name__,
                            "MsixMemRestoreMutated")

    if os.path.islink(drv_link):
        orig_driver = os.path.basename(os.path.realpath(drv_link))
        try:
            glt_utils.write_sysfs_value(
                f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/driver/unbind", bdf)
        except OSError as e:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(
                f"could not unbind {orig_driver} from {bdf}: {e}")
    try:
        glt_utils.write_sysfs_value(
            f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/driver_override", "vfio-pci")
        glt_utils.write_sysfs_value("/sys/bus/pci/drivers/vfio-pci/bind", bdf)
    except OSError as e:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(f"could not bind {bdf} to vfio-pci: {e}")
    if (not os.path.islink(drv_link)
            or os.path.basename(os.path.realpath(drv_link)) != "vfio-pci"):
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(f"{bdf} did not bind to vfio-pci")
    logger.info("%s bound to vfio-pci", bdf)

    vf_token = str(uuid.uuid4())
    try:
        # pylint: disable-next=consider-using-with
        proc = subprocess.Popen(
            ["vfio_mlx5", f"--device={bdf},vf_token={vf_token}",
             "--memsize=1G"],
            stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    except OSError as e:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(f"could not launch vfio_mlx5: {e}")

    try:
        lspci_out = ""
        msix_enabled = False
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 60.0
        while time.monotonic() < deadline:
            if proc.poll() is not None:
                GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(
                    f"vfio_mlx5 exited early (rc={proc.returncode}) before "
                    f"enabling MSI-X on {bdf}")
            try:
                result = subprocess.run(["lspci", "-vv", "-s", bdf],
                                        capture_output=True, text=True,
                                        check=False)
                lspci_out = result.stdout if result.returncode == 0 else ""
            except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
                lspci_out = ""
            if "MSI-X: Enable+" in lspci_out:
                msix_enabled = True
                break
            time.sleep(1)
        if not msix_enabled:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(
                f"vfio_mlx5 did not enable MSI-X on {bdf} within 60s")

        # BAR0 base + MSI-X vector-table offset, for log attribution only.
        bar0 = re.search(r"Region 0: Memory at ([0-9a-f]+)", lspci_out)
        table = re.search(r"Vector table: BAR=(\d+) offset=([0-9a-f]+)",
                          lspci_out)
        logger.info(
            "MSI-X enabled on %s (BAR0=%s, vector table BAR=%s offset=0x%s)",
            bdf,
            bar0.group(1) if bar0 else "?",
            table.group(1) if table else "?",
            table.group(2) if table else "?")

        try:
            checkpoint = glt_utils.capture_kernel_log_checkpoint()
        except RuntimeError as error:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(
                f"Failed to capture kernel log checkpoint before FLR on "
                f"{bdf}: {error}"
            )

        command = _setpci_read_word(bdf, pci_command_offset)
        if command is None:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(
                f"could not read COMMAND on {bdf} via setpci")

        if not _setpci_write_word(bdf, pci_command_offset,
                                  command & ~pci_command_memory):
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(f"failed to clear COMMAND.Memory on {bdf}")
        readback = _setpci_read_word(bdf, pci_command_offset)
        if readback is None or readback & pci_command_memory:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip(
                f"COMMAND.Memory did not clear on {bdf} "
                f"(read back {'unreadable' if readback is None else hex(readback)})")

        # FLR is the chosen reliable trigger for this regression. There might be
        # other reset paths that could hit the MSI-X path under test.
        logger.info("Triggering FLR on %s", bdf)
        try:
            subprocess.run(
                ["sh", "-c", f"echo 1 > {dev_path}/reset"],
                capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=120)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(
                f"FLR write on {bdf} did not complete within 120s")
        except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(
                f"FLR write on {bdf} failed (rc={e.returncode}): "
                f"{(e.stderr or '').strip()}")
        except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError) as e:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(f"FLR could not be issued on {bdf} ({e})")

        try:
            with open(f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/config", "rb") as cfg:
                vendor = cfg.read(2)
            speed = glt_utils.read_sysfs_value(
                f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/current_link_speed")
            healthy = (len(vendor) == 2 and vendor != b"\xff\xff"
                       and not speed.startswith("Unknown"))
        except OSError:
            healthy = False

        try:
            kernel_log = glt_utils.get_kernel_log(checkpoint)
        except RuntimeError as error:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(
                f"Failed to retrieve kernel log after FLR on {bdf}: {error}"
            )

        for signature in fault_signatures:
            if signature in kernel_log:
                logger.error("fault signature in kernel log: %s", signature)
                GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(patch_fail_msg)

        if not healthy:
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(
                "device did not recover after FLR "
                "(config inaccessible / link down)")

        logger.info("FLR completed cleanly on %s; no UR/DPC/AER signature", bdf)
    finally:
        proc.terminate()
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=10)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            proc.kill()
            proc.wait()

# Development Setup Guide

This guide covers setting up a local environment to work **on** GreenLiT itself
(running lint, running unit tests, iterating on source). If you instead want to
**install and use** GreenLiT to run tests against a target system, see the
[README](../../README.md#getting-started) — Option A (`install.sh`) for a
normal install, or Option B for an offline/wheel-based install.

## Index

- [Requirements](#requirements)
- [Setting up a Development Environment](#setting-up-a-development-environment)
- [Running Local Checks](#running-local-checks)
- [Manual Runtime Configuration](#manual-runtime-configuration)
- [Building Release Wheels (Poetry)](#building-release-wheels-poetry)
- [Managing Declared Dependencies (Poetry)](#managing-declared-dependencies-poetry)
- [Coding Style](#coding-style)

## Requirements

- Python 3.10 or higher
- Clone the greenlit repository or untar the source tarball
- Root/sudo privileges, but only if you go on to do the optional
  [manual runtime configuration](#manual-runtime-configuration) below

## Setting up a Development Environment

The recommended day-to-day workflow uses a plain `venv` named `gltenv` and
`pip install .` — this mirrors the setup CI uses to lint and test every
change, so running it locally closely reproduces CI.

One-time setup:

```bash
python3 -m venv gltenv && source gltenv/bin/activate && pip install --trusted-host pypi.org --trusted-host files.pythonhosted.org . pylint pytest pytest-cov
```

The `--trusted-host` flags disable certificate verification for those hosts,
which is only safe on a network where the path to PyPI is otherwise trusted
(e.g. behind a corporate TLS-inspecting proxy). Drop them if your network
reaches PyPI directly.

Re-activate `gltenv` (`source gltenv/bin/activate`) in each new shell before
running the checks below.

## Running Local Checks

Run these before creating a commit or MR. Skip any check whose tool isn't
installed. `shellcheck` and `jq` are system tools; `pylint` and `pytest` come
from the `gltenv` venv set up above. [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) points here
for the canonical local-check commands.

| Tool | Command |
|------|---------|
| Python lint | `source gltenv/bin/activate && find . -not -path "./gltenv/*" -name "*.py" -print0 \| xargs -0 pylint --init-hook="import sys; sys.path.extend(['src', '.'])"` |
| Shell lint | `find . -name "*.sh" -print0 \| xargs -0 shellcheck` |
| JSON validation | `find . -name "*.json" -print0 \| xargs -0 jq -r . > /dev/null` |
| Unit tests | `source gltenv/bin/activate && python -m pytest tests/ -v --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing` |

## Manual Runtime Configuration

`pip install .` only installs the Python package — it does not stage private
runtime helpers, runtime configuration files, or systemd units that a real
GreenLiT install needs. `install.sh` does all of this automatically for end
users (see the [README](../../README.md)); if you're testing runtime/service
integration against a `pip install .`-based dev checkout without running the
full installer, stage it manually:

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/greenlit/{bin,confs.d,executing_dir}
sudo cp -R src/bin/. /usr/share/greenlit/bin/
sudo cp confs/hardware-manifest.json /usr/share/greenlit/
sudo cp confs/glt-confs.d/* /usr/share/greenlit/confs.d/
sudo cp -r external_tests/* /usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir/

# Set up systemd services
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/systemd/system
sudo cp confs/greenlit.service /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/
sudo cp confs/greenlit.timer /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```

Poetry is used for exporting dependency metadata when packaging distributable
wheels (e.g. the offline install bundle described in the README's
[Option B](../../README.md#option-b-offline-installation)) — it is **not**
part of the day-to-day dev/lint/test loop above.

```bash

# an unverified remote installer straight into sudo)
```

## Managing Declared Dependencies (Poetry)

GreenLiT's runtime and packaging dependencies are declared in
`pyproject.toml`. Use Poetry to manage that file — these commands affect what
gets packaged (and what `pip install .` pulls in), not a separate Poetry-based
dev environment:

```bash
# Add a runtime dependency
poetry add pyyaml

# Update dependencies
poetry update

# Show current dependencies
poetry show
```

**Note**: `poetry add`, `poetry remove`, and `poetry update` automatically
generate `poetry.lock` — remove it manually, since GreenLiT intentionally does
not lock package versions.

## Coding Style

When adding or refactoring functions, keep them in alphabetical order within
their local section unless lifecycle, dependency, or framework ordering is
clearer. This applies to source files and related unit tests.

# Makefile for FEAT_LS64 test programs

# Detect host architecture
HOST_ARCH := $(shell uname -m)

# Compiler selection
ifeq ($(HOST_ARCH),aarch64)
    # Native ARM64 build
    CC ?= gcc
    $(info Building natively for aarch64)
else
    # Cross-compile for ARM64
    CC := aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc
    $(info Cross-compiling from $(HOST_ARCH) to aarch64)
endif

CFLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -O2 -g
LDFLAGS =

# Target binary
TARGET = test_ls64

# Source files
SRC = test_ls64.c

# Object files
OBJ = $(SRC:.c=.o)

.PHONY: all clean run

all: $(TARGET)

$(TARGET): $(OBJ)
	$(CC) $(LDFLAGS) -o $@ $^

%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<

run: $(TARGET)
	./$(TARGET)

clean:
	rm -f $(TARGET) $(OBJ)

obj-m := test_dma_alloc.o

KDIR ?= /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build

all:
	$(MAKE) -C $(KDIR) M=$(PWD) modules

clean:
	$(MAKE) -C $(KDIR) M=$(PWD) clean

## Introduction & Objectives

A quick step-by-step guide for those who need to create GreenLiT test cases and get them running in test cycles, without deep-diving into the logic behind how GreenLiT manages the test case execution.

**Note**: This doc will not focus on any development process related topics. For those please refer to the prerequisites section.

## Prerequisites

Before creating test cases, you should have:

- An understanding of **GreenLiT Development Process** for how to:
  - Create working branches
  - Create an issue/ticket ID to ensure the change is used to address that issue.
  - Go through merge request process
- Background knowledge on **Python**

## Do We Need a New Test Case?

Before creating a new test case, check if existing test cases cover what you'd like to test.

"Existing" meaning:

- The GreenLiT specific tests located in GreenLiT repository, **or**
- Upstream kselftests that are included in test cycles

There will be no need to create a duplicated test case if either of the above two already covers what you'd like to check.

## Choosing the Implementation Path

GreenLiT supports both native Python tests and standalone executable tests.
Choose the implementation path based on how the test should be run, maintained,
and integrated with the framework.

Prefer a native GreenLiT Python test under
`src/modules/<category>/glt_test_<feature>.py` when possible. Native tests can
use GreenLiT decorators, test plans, dependencies, scheduler state, post hooks,
common helpers, and consistent skip/fail handling.

GreenLiT also supports standalone executable tests for cases where another test
suite or validation script already exists. During installation, files from the
repository's `external_tests/` directory are copied into the installed external
test directory, `/usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir`. Users can also place their
own executable tests in that installed directory, or use `glt-test-suite
--ext-dir <path>`, without contributing those tests to the GreenLiT repository.

External executable tests let users run native GreenLiT tests and standalone
tests with a single `glt-test-suite` command and collect one report format.

The `external_tests/` name describes the execution mechanism: GreenLiT launches
an executable from the external test directory instead of discovering a
decorated Python test under `src/modules/`. For tests submitted to the GreenLiT
repository, this does not change the normal contribution or review process.

For tests contributed to the GreenLiT repository, treat `external_tests/` as an
integration and staging path, not the preferred long-term home for
GreenLiT-specific test logic. If the test should reuse GreenLiT framework
features or APIs from `src/common/`, plan to migrate the logic into a native
Python test under `src/modules/`.

### When Starting from an Existing Script

When an existing shell, Python, or binary validation script is provided, first
decide whether the script's logic should be converted into a native test or
staged as a standalone executable:

- Check whether existing GreenLiT tests or upstream kselftests already cover the same behavior. If they partially cover it, extend the existing test instead of adding a duplicate.
- If the test validates a kernel, firmware, or userspace patch, review the related patch or source repository when available so the test checks the intended behavior instead of only reproducing the script structure.
- Convert to a native Python test when the test needs GreenLiT helpers, dependencies, scheduler state, reboot handling, post hooks, multiple test plans, or reusable framework logic.
- Before adding local helpers, adapters, or launchers, check `src/common/` and nearby module utilities. Reuse or extend existing helpers when the behavior already exists or is likely to be reused.
- Consider `external_tests/` as a staging path when short-term integration is needed, the script is already maintained as a separate executable test, or the script already fits GreenLiT's standalone executable contract.
- Preserve the script's intended pass/fail/skip behavior when converting it or adapting it for `external_tests/`.
- If the script needs arguments, environment variables, setup/cleanup, or result-code translation, provide a small adapter that normalizes those details for GreenLiT. A launcher that only invokes the script without adapting anything usually does not improve integration.

Standalone executable scripts are case-by-case. For repository submissions,
document the prerequisites, required tools, root or hardware assumptions,
arguments, environment variables, setup and cleanup steps, and result mapping.

## Unit Tests

Add unit tests for hardware-independent framework, CLI, parser, scheduler, or helper logic. Hardware-dependent test cases under `src/modules/` may rely on targeted review or hardware validation instead, but shared logic should be covered under `tests/` when practical.

## Create a Test Case that Does Not Require Reboots

Please refer to any test case (i.e. a function that starts with `test_` under `<category>/glt_test_<feature>.py`) for more examples.

### Example Test Case Structure

The basic contents of a test case would look like the following code block. While you could simply make copies of existing tests and start your test case creation journey from there, scroll down further and refer to the breakdown of this piece of code to understand what each section means, and how you can use them to design your test case:

```python
from common import glt_core as GLTCore
from common import glt_utils
from common.nv_device import NvDev

EXPECTED_MODEL_NAME = "Olympus"

@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("standard")
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("stress")
def test_vera_lscpu_model_name(_, logger):
    """
    Test if the Vera CPU model name is Olympus.

    PATCH: https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commit/9087774
    """
    nvdev = NvDev()
    if not nvdev.is_cpu_type("vera"):
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("The CPU is not Vera.")

    model_name = glt_utils.get_cpu_model_name(logger)
    if model_name is None:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail("Failed to get CPU model name from lscpu.")

    logger.info("lscpu Model name: %s", model_name)

    if EXPECTED_MODEL_NAME != model_name:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(
            f"CPU model name mismatch. Expected '{EXPECTED_MODEL_NAME}' in model name, "
            f"but got '{model_name}'. "
            "Please backport the patch to util-linux: "
            "https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commit/9087774"
        )
```

### Categorizing Your Test Case

#### Step 1: Decide which category your test case should fit in

- Existing categories can be found [here](../../src/modules/)
- Under your preferred category, locate which `glt_test_<feature>.py` you'd like to host your test case in and add your new test case there
- Create a new `glt_test_<feature>.py` if needed

#### Step 2: Creating a new category (if needed)

In rare scenarios where none of the existing categories fits your needs, create new ones by duplicating and modifying existing files and directories.

When any new "category" (i.e. new directory under `/src/modules`) is introduced, **Update GreenLiT architecture.md** to contain information about your new category is required.

### Choosing Test Plans

Decide which test plan(s) your test case should be included into.

Choose from the 3 valid native test plans:

- `"standard"` - Comprehensive non-disruptive validation; tests must not
  intentionally reboot or kexec and must not be reasonably expected to hang,
  crash, reset, or require manual recovery
- `"disruptive"` - Tests that intentionally reboot or kexec the system, or might
  hang or crash it only if a required patch is missing. Manual recovery, such as
  a power cycle, might be required
- `"stress"` - Extended stress and stability testing; may include disruptive
  tests

Use the decorator `@GLTCore.GLTPlan("<test plan name>")` with your test case to include the test into a certain plan. Use multiple decorators if your test should be in multiple test plans.
Do not assign the same test to both `standard` and `disruptive`. Disruptive
tests should normally also remain in `stress` when extended validation is
appropriate.

**Example:**

```python
@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("standard")
def test_my_feature(_, logger):
    """Test description"""
    # test implementation
```

### Naming and Formatting Rules

- **One test case = one function**
  - Refrain from testing multiple features within one function/test case unless there's a reason to do so

- **Test case names must start with `test_`** and follow the pattern:
  ```python
  test_<feature>(sd, logger):
  ```
  
  Where:
  - `sd` - "scheduler" (likely needed if your test steps contain a reboot)
  - `logger` - for when you need to record additional logs throughout the test

- **If either one (or none) is not needed for your test**, replace arguments with placeholders for consistency in test case function signatures:
  ```python
  test_<feature>(sd, _)    # Only need scheduler
  test_<feature>(_, logger) # Only need logger
  test_<feature>(_, __)     # Need neither
  ```

#### Docstring Requirements

**Required elements:**

- Short description of what is tested
- Include link to related backport patch(es) if available

**Example:**

```python
def test_vera_lscpu_model_name(_, logger):
    """
    Test if the Vera CPU model name is Olympus.

    PATCH: https://github.com/util-linux/util-linux/commit/9087774
    """
```

#### Handling Known Bugs and TODOs

Use a comment above the line that requires modifying:

```python
# FIXME DGX-5678 <issue description>
```

### Using GLTTestAttr

`@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()` collects and stores test case attributes. **Please wrap your test case function with it.**

```python
@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("standard")
def test_my_feature(_, logger):
    """Test description"""
    pass
```

### Leveraging GreenLiT Utilities

Various functions and methods are available under:

- **`glt_utils`**: General Linux related utilities
  - Example: Check if command/tool is available in the DUT
- **`nv_device`**: NVIDIA specific utilities
  - Example: Check if CPU is Grace

**Important:** Chances are a command you'd like to use in your test case has a ready-to-be-called function available in the above modules. Use those instead of creating your own to prevent reinventing the wheel.

If existing functions under these modules require an update to fit your needs, or if you feel that the commands you are about to use would likely be reused in other test cases in the future, instead of creating the steps inside your new test case, please update these modules and have your test case call them.

Apply the same rule to helper code and adapters. Before adding a local wrapper,
launcher, parser, or setup helper inside a test file, check `src/common/` and
nearby module utilities first. Keep helper logic local only when it is specific
to that one test and unlikely to be reused.

### Running CLI Commands with `run_command`

Use `glt_utils.run_command()` for the common CLI case: an argv list whose text
stdout is needed, a non-zero exit is a failure, and one domain-specific
message is enough for the caller. The helper always uses `shell=False`,
captures text output, checks the return code, and applies a 30s timeout unless
`timeout` is overridden.

Timeout, non-zero exit, and decode failures raise
`RuntimeError(failure_message)`. An executable that cannot start raises
`RuntimeError(f"Failed to run {command[0]}")`. Test cases typically catch
`RuntimeError` and pass `str(error)` to `GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail()`:

```python
try:
    result = glt_utils.run_command(
        ["lspci", "-Dv"],
        "Failed to enumerate PCI devices with 'lspci'",
    )
except RuntimeError as error:
    GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(str(error))
```

Keep a direct `subprocess.run()` call when the caller needs a non-zero return
code, redirected or binary output, stdin, unbounded runtime, or the
original subprocess exception rather than a `RuntimeError`.

### Using GLTLibvirt for Virtualization Tests

Use `common.virt.glt_libvirt.GLTLibvirt` when a test case needs to create or
manage local libvirt/QEMU domains. The helper centralizes `virsh` invocation,
domain XML generation, debug logging, and common cleanup behavior.

Before using it, fail or skip early if virtualization tools are unavailable:

```python
if not glt_utils.is_cli_available("virsh"):
    GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail("Please install 'virsh' to perform the test.")
```

Create the helper with the test logger. The constructor validates that `virsh`
can connect to `qemu:///system`, so catch `ConnectionError` and convert it to a
GreenLiT test result:

```python
try:
    libvirt_conn = GLTLibvirt(logger=logger)
except ConnectionError as e:
    GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(str(e))
```

For direct-kernel boot domains, build XML through `generate_domain_xml()` and
use `define_and_start()` for the common define/start flow:

```python
from common.virt.glt_libvirt import GLTLibvirt


@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("stress")
def test_my_virtualization_case(_, logger):
    domain_name = "glt-my-test-vm"
    libvirt_conn = GLTLibvirt(logger=logger)
    xml_config = libvirt_conn.generate_domain_xml({
        "domain_name": domain_name,
        "memory_mb": 512,
        "vcpus": 4,
        "arch": "aarch64",
        "kernel_path": "/var/lib/libvirt/boot/Image",
        "initrd_path": "",
        "kernel_args": "console=ttyAMA0 rdinit=/bin/sh panic=0",
    })

    try:
        if not libvirt_conn.define_and_start(xml_config):
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(f"Failed to start {domain_name}")

        success, output, _ = libvirt_conn.run_virsh_command(["domstate", domain_name])
        if not success or "running" not in output.lower():
            GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(f"{domain_name} is not running: {output}")
    finally:
        libvirt_conn.cleanup(domain_name)
```

Guidelines:

- Always clean up domains in a `finally` block. A failed test should not leave
  `glt-*` domains behind for later test runs.
- Use `define_and_start()` for the normal single-domain flow. Use `define()` and
  `start()` separately only when a test needs to inspect or modify the domain
  between those steps.
- If a test creates many domains, destroy all domains first and then undefine
  them. This mirrors stress scenarios where teardown fanout is part of the
  behavior under test.
- Keep generated kernel/initrd artifacts in a path libvirt can read, such as
  `/var/lib/libvirt/boot`, and remove staged artifacts after the test.
- The helper manages host-side libvirt only. Do not add guest command execution
  APIs until a real test case needs them and the guest access method is clear.

### Test Results: FAILED, SKIPPED, or WARNING

Use `glt_core`'s test result methods to tell GreenLiT to fail, skip, or warn from a test:

```python
GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("<skip reason>")
GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail("<error message>")
GLTCore.GLTTestResult.warn("<advisory message>")
```

Use `warn()` when the test detects an advisory condition — something worth surfacing in the report but not a hard failure (e.g., a deprecated configuration, a suboptimal-but-functional hardware state). Like `skip()` and `fail()`, `warn()` stops the test immediately and must only be called from a function decorated with `@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()`.

**By default**, if none of the conditions required to skip, fail, or warn are met, the test case **passes**.

**See also**: [Appendix: Allowing test result exceptions](#appendix-allowing-test-result-exceptions) for how to dynamically allow certain cases to be skipped and failed cases to not count towards fails. Note that these circumstances are usually special-case scenarios where the fail/skip criteria is not a long term logic that should go into the main test case function (e.g., ignore failure during bug fix period).

### Managing Test Case Dependencies

#### Must Pass Dependency

`@GLTCore.GLTRequires.must_pass("<category>", "<test case>")`

If your test case should only be run when other test case(s) have passed, wrap your test case with this decorator, where:
- `<category>` is the category of the case that must pass first
- `<test case>` is the name of the test case that must pass first

#### Must Fail Dependency

`@GLTCore.GLTRequires.must_fail("<category>", "<test case>")`

If your test case should only be run when other test case(s) have failed, use this decorator instead.

#### Example

```python
@GLTCore.GLTRequires.must_pass("hwtracing", "test_perf_coresight")
@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("standard")
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("stress")
def test_nvidia_perf_events(_, logger):
    """Test NVIDIA perf events"""
    # ...(section omitted for brevity)
    
    # FIXME: perf seems not enable coresight on ubuntu.
    if NvDev.get_release_info().get("NAME") == "Ubuntu":
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.skip("Perf doesn't enable coresight on Ubuntu.")
    
    # ...(section omitted for brevity)
```

### Post-Test Actions with Post Hooks

When a test needs to run something after it completes (e.g. cleanup, teardown, or restore), use **post hooks**. The framework supports five hooks currently, one per outcome: `postsuccess` (test passed), `postskip` (test skipped), `postfail` (test failed), `postafail` (allowed failure), `postwarn` (test warned). After the test, the runner invokes the matching hook.

**How to use:** Create a `PostHooks` instance with `GLTCore.PostHooks.create(postsuccess=..., postskip=..., postfail=..., postafail=..., postwarn=...)` and assign it to your test's **attr**: `test_something.attr.post_hooks = ...`. Pass callables with signature `(scheduler, attr, logger)` for the outcomes you need. Any slot you omit is a no-op. Each test has its own post hooks on its own attr; only tests that set `attr.post_hooks` get post hooks run. Example:

```python
def test_something(sd, logger):
    ...

test_something.attr.post_hooks = GLTCore.PostHooks.create(postsuccess=my_cleanup_fn)
```

You can pass the same or different callables for each outcome. For a full example that uses hooks to restore after a reboot, see [Create a Test Case that Requires Reboots](#create-a-test-case-that-requires-reboots).

## Create a Test Case that Requires Reboots

Some tests need to reboot the device under test and resume after boot to check
post-reboot state, or need a special reboot mechanism to recover from a locked-up
kernel. All reboot mechanisms rely on the same pattern: check `sd.progress` to tell
whether this is the first run or a resumed run after the test triggered its own
reboot, as shown in the
[Create a Test Case that Requires a Simple Reboot](#create-a-test-case-that-requires-a-simple-reboot)
example below.

### Create a Test Case that Requires a Simple Reboot

Use `glt_utils.reboot()` for a plain reboot with no special kernel command line
changes. Record progress before rebooting so the resumed run knows it already
triggered the reboot:

```python
@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("disruptive")
@GLTCore.GLTPlan("stress")
def test_reboot(sd, logger):
    """Reboot system to see if it's bootable"""
    for tests in sd.progress:
        if test_reboot.__name__ not in tests:
            continue
        if "TriggerReboot" not in tests[test_reboot.__name__]:
            logger.debug("Rebooting...")
            ret = glt_utils.reboot(test_reboot.__name__, sd)
            if ret is False:
                GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail("Failed to trigger GLT reboot")
        else:
            logger.debug("Rebooted and resume successfully.")
            glt_utils.systemd_enable(enable=False)
```

(from `src/modules/power/glt_test_power_cycle.py`.) `glt_utils.reboot()` does not
return on success — it records progress and triggers `reboot` (or, in development
mode without systemd, sends itself `SIGTERM` to emulate shutdown). It only returns
`False` if it could not trigger the reboot at all.

For kernel lockup / hang recovery scenarios where a clean `reboot` may not respond,
use `glt_utils.reboot_with_reisub()` instead. It triggers a SysRq REISUB sequence
(sync filesystems, remount read-only, reboot) rather than a normal shutdown, so it
can recover the system even when standard shutdown paths are unresponsive.

### Create a Test Case that Requires kexec Reboots

Some tests need to kexec into a modified kernel command line, run the
actual test logic after kexec, and then reboot back to a clean state so
remaining tests can proceed. Use `glt_utils.handle_kexec_flow()` to
manage the three-phase kexec lifecycle:

1. **Verify prior attempt** — If a previous kexec was triggered but the
   system did not kexec-boot, the function returns `(False, reason)`.
2. **Initiate kexec** — If the system has not kexec-booted yet, the
   function calls `reboot_with_kexec()`. The process exits and the
   framework does not run more tests in that session.
3. **Resume after kexec** — On the next run, the framework resumes and
   `handle_kexec_flow()` detects the kexec boot. It disables the systemd
   service and returns `(True, None)`, signalling the test to proceed
   with its actual logic.

When `handle_kexec_flow()` returns `(False, reason)`, pass `reason` to
`GLTTestResult.fail()`. When it returns `(True, None)`, the kexec boot
was successful and the test should proceed with its actual logic.

#### Conditional reboot after kexec

After the test completes (pass, fail, or allowed-failure), the system
should reboot back to normal boot. Use
`PostHooks.for_conditional_reboot("TriggerKexec", glt_utils.is_kexec_boot)`
to register a post-hook that triggers a reboot only when the system is
in a kexec-booted state. Register it for `postsuccess`, `postfail`, and
`postafail`. Omit `postskip` (default no-op) because a skip means kexec
was never triggered.

#### Example

See `test_efi_runtime_services_mask` in `src/modules/acpi/glt_test_efi.py`
(module-level imports of `GLTCore` and `glt_utils` omitted for brevity — see
[Example Test Case Structure](#example-test-case-structure) above):

```python
_kexec_conditional_reboot_hook = GLTCore.PostHooks.for_conditional_reboot(
    "TriggerKexec",
    glt_utils.is_kexec_boot,
)

@GLTCore.GLTTestAttr()

    ok, reason = glt_utils.handle_kexec_flow(
        test_efi_runtime_services_mask.__name__, sd, logger,
    )
    if not ok:
        GLTCore.GLTTestResult.fail(reason)

    # Actual test logic runs here (only reached after kexec boot)
```

that need extra kernel command line arguments, e.g.
`handle_kexec_flow(test_name, sd, logger, custom_cmdline="pci=config_acs=101xxxx@0000:00:01.0")`.

## Create an External Test Case

External tests are standalone executable scripts (shell, Python, or any
executable) that run outside the native GreenLiT Python test framework but are
automatically discovered and executed by GreenLiT.

The repository's `external_tests/` directory is packaged with GreenLiT. During
installation, its contents are copied to `/usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir`,
which is the default external test directory used by `glt-test-suite`. Users can
also add their own executable tests directly under
`/usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir`, or point `glt-test-suite` at a different
directory with `--ext-dir <path>`.

This allows GreenLiT to launch native test cases and standalone executable tests
from one `glt-test-suite` command and collect one report format. Adding tests to
the installed external test directory does not require contributing them to the
GreenLiT repository.

The term "external" describes the implementation mechanism only. For tests
submitted to the GreenLiT repository, standalone executable tests follow the
same contribution and review process as other test changes.

### When to Use External Tests

Use external tests when:
- You have existing test scripts that don't fit into the Python test framework
- You need to write tests in bash or other scripting languages
- You want to integrate third-party test tools
- Your test is a one-off or experimental test
- You prefer a simpler approach without Python decorators and GreenLiT utilities
- You need a short-term staging path before converting the logic into a native
  GreenLiT Python test

Before choosing this path, confirm the script can be launched without hidden
assumptions. If it needs command-line arguments, special environment variables,
setup/cleanup, non-standard result codes, or tighter interaction with GreenLiT
state, either provide a small adapter with clear documentation or convert the
logic into a native Python test.

For GreenLiT-specific test logic, prefer migrating from `external_tests/` into
`src/modules/` over time so the test can reuse the framework and common helper
APIs.

### Directory Structure

For tests contributed to the GreenLiT repository, external tests are placed in
the `external_tests/` directory:

```
greenlit/
└── external_tests/
    ├── tpm/
    │   └── test_config_tcg_tis_spi.sh
    └── your_category/
        └── your_test_script.sh
```

After installation, repository external tests are copied to
`/usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir`. For local-only or site-specific executable
tests, place them directly under `/usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir` on the
device under test, or run `glt-test-suite --ext-dir <path>`.

### Exit Codes

External tests communicate their results through exit codes:

| Exit Code | Status | Description |
|-----------|--------|-------------|
| `0` | PASS | Test passed successfully |
| `1` | FAIL | Test failed |
| `2` | XFAIL | Expected failure (test is expected to fail and did fail) |
| `3` | XPASS | Unexpected pass (test is expected to fail but passed - counts as FAIL) |
| `4` | SKIP | Test should be skipped |

### Creating an External Test

#### Step 1: Create Your Test Script

For a repository contribution, create an executable script in
`external_tests/`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# external_tests/my_category/test_my_feature.sh

# Perform your test
if some_command_that_tests_your_feature; then
    echo "Test passed: Feature is working correctly"
    exit 0  # PASS
else
    echo "Test failed: Feature is not working"
    exit 1  # FAIL
fi
```

#### Step 2: Make It Executable

```bash
chmod +x external_tests/my_category/test_my_feature.sh
```

#### Step 3: Test Your Script

Run it manually to verify:

```bash
./external_tests/my_category/test_my_feature.sh
echo $?  # Check exit code
```

### Example External Test Scripts

#### Example 1: Simple Bash Test

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# external_tests/storage/test_disk_space.sh

# Check if we have at least 1GB free space
free_space=$(df -BG / | awk 'NR==2 {print $4}' | sed 's/G//')

if [ "$free_space" -ge 1 ]; then
    echo "PASS: Free space is ${free_space}GB"
    exit 0
else
    echo "FAIL: Insufficient free space: ${free_space}GB"
    exit 1
fi
```

#### Example 2: Python External Test

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# external_tests/network/test_dns_resolution.sh

import socket
import sys

def test_dns():
    try:
        socket.gethostbyname('www.google.com')
        print("PASS: DNS resolution working")
        return 0
    except socket.gaierror:
        print("FAIL: DNS resolution failed")
        return 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(test_dns())
```

#### Example 3: Test with Expected Failure

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# external_tests/experimental/test_new_feature.sh

# This feature is known to be broken on certain kernels
if test_new_feature; then
    echo "Feature is working"
    exit 0  # PASS
else
    # Check if this is a known issue
    if uname -r | grep -q "5.15"; then
        echo "Expected failure on kernel 5.15"
        exit 2  # XFAIL (expected failure)
    else
        echo "Unexpected failure"
        exit 1  # FAIL
    fi
fi
```

#### Example 4: Test with Skip Logic

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# external_tests/hardware/test_tpm_device.sh

# Check if TPM hardware is available
if [ ! -e /dev/tpm0 ]; then
    echo "SKIP: TPM device not found"
    exit 4  # SKIP
fi

# Run the actual test
if tpm_test_command; then
    echo "PASS: TPM test successful"
    exit 0
else
    echo "FAIL: TPM test failed"
    exit 1
fi
```

### Test Discovery

GreenLiT automatically discovers external tests by:

1. Recursively scanning the `external_tests/` directory
2. Finding all executable files
3. Processing subdirectories first (depth-first search)
4. Executing tests in alphabetical order

**Test naming convention:**
- The test name is derived from the relative path
- Example: `external_tests/tpm/test_config.sh` becomes `external:tpm_test_config_sh`

### Environment Variables

External tests can access the following environment variable:

- **`GTL_WORKDIR`**: Working directory for the test to store temporary files or logs

**Example usage:**

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Use GTL_WORKDIR for temporary files
temp_file="${GTL_WORKDIR}/temp_data.txt"
echo "Test data" > "$temp_file"
# Perform test using temp_file
```

### Best Practices

1. **Use descriptive names**: Name your test scripts clearly (e.g., `test_feature_name.sh`)

2. **Provide clear output**: Always echo what the test is doing and why it passed/failed

3. **Check prerequisites**: Use exit code 4 (SKIP) if required hardware/software is not available

4. **Handle errors gracefully**: Use proper error checking and return appropriate exit codes

5. **Keep tests focused**: One test per script, testing one specific feature

6. **Document your test**: Add comments explaining what the test does and any prerequisites

7. **Test locally first**: Always run your external test manually before committing

### Organizing External Tests

You can organize external tests in subdirectories by category:

```
external_tests/
├── hardware/
│   ├── test_cpu.sh
│   └── test_memory.sh
├── network/
│   ├── test_connectivity.sh
│   └── test_dns.sh
└── storage/
    └── test_disk_io.sh
```

### Limitations

External tests have some limitations compared to Python test cases:

- Cannot use GreenLiT utilities (`glt_utils`, `nv_device`, etc.)
- Cannot use test dependencies (`@GLTRequires`)
- Limited to single test plan (`ext_executable`)
- No direct access to the scheduler for reboot testing
- Must manage their own error handling and logging

If your test needs these features, create a native Python test under
`src/modules/` and assign `disruptive` and `stress` when it needs reboot or
kexec handling.

## Inclusion of Additional Packages

If your test case requires additional packages that aren't available by default in the device-under-test:

### Case A: Packages Installable via Package Manager

- Install packages via the test device's package manager directly(e.g., `apt`, `dnf`, `zypper`).

### Case B: Executables Not Available via Package Manager

Executables that cannot be installed through a distro's software management system.

**Required steps:**

1. Put all files under the same parent as your `glt_test_<feature>.py` file, i.e., the root directory of your selected category (e.g., `/src/modules/i2c`).

2. Update GreenLiT `pyproject.toml` to include your package(s) and files if they are not Python-based.

## Licensing Considerations

Beware of potential licensing issues when including third-party packages or
code. GreenLiT is a public project, so contributions should not include
non-public, embargoed, confidential, or otherwise sensitive implementation
details. If you are unsure whether a test belongs in the public repository, ask
before submitting it.

## Follow Ups

Your test case should make it into the next GreenLiT release, which roughly follows a **1-month cadence**, after an MR is merged.

## Appendix: Allowing Test Result Exceptions

While each test case contains code that controls when to skip or fail a test in "normal" situations, there are times where one needs to temporarily allow a case to either be skipped or the failure masked.

### Use Case Example

A bug that causes test case `test_all_pmu_events` to fail was introduced in the latest release of Ubuntu, but won't be fixed until the next release.

We might not want that case to keep showing up as failing during this bug fix period as it:
- Introduces unnecessary noise to test reports, or
- Blocks test cycles when the failure is a known, tracked issue awaiting an upstream fix

### Solution: Configuration YAML Files

`.yaml` files following the `00_default.yaml` format allow you to solve this problem, **without touching the actual test cases themselves**.

#### Step 1: Create or Update Configuration

Update the contents of `00_default.yaml` directly, or maintain your own set of separate `.yaml` files:

```yaml
arm64:test_all_pmu_events:
  allow-failure:
    - condition:
        name: "Perf is not ready on Ubuntu 20.04"
        distro: "Ubuntu"
        release: "20.04"
    - condition:
        name: "Coresight is not ready on Redhat 9.5"
        distro: "Red Hat"
        release: "9.5"
  conditional-skip:
    - condition:
        name: "Skip because is not ready on Ubuntu 20.04"
        distro: "Ubuntu"
        release: "20.04"
    - condition:
        name: "Just a test"
        script: |
          #!/bin/bash
          grep -q 'nfs' /proc/cmdline
```

### Configuration Breakdown

**Format:** `<category>:<test_case_name>`
- Example: `arm64:test_all_pmu_events`
- This identifies the test case that requires conditional result changes

**Alternative Results:**
There are 2 valid alternatives:
- **`allow-failure`**: Keeps the failed outcome of the test case, but does not count towards "failed"
- **`conditional-skip`**: Will result in the test case not being run

**Condition Fields:**
- **`name`**: Please put in the reason you're applying "allow-failure" or "conditional-skip"
- **Conditions can be based on:**
  - **Distribution** (`distro` and `release`)
  - **Script execution** (`script`) - whether a script returns True

#### Step 2: Deploy Configuration

Copy your `.yaml` file(s) to the device under test's `/usr/share/greenlit/confs.d` directory.

- Multiple files are allowed and will all be detected and applied
- Your next rounds of tests' test results should reflect the configurations set in these `.yaml` files

    apt update

      echo "3. Search available headers: apt search linux-headers-$(uname -r | cut -d'-' -f1)"
    fi

    echo "Installing required system packages..."

    echo "Installing required system packages..."
    zypper --non-interactive refresh
    zypper --non-interactive install python3-pip tar ipmitool perf freeipmi kernel-default-devel linux-glibc-devel libgpiod stress-ng kexec-tools
    zypper --non-interactive install bpftrace || echo "WARNING: bpftrace unavailable; CMDQV tests will not run"
    zypper --non-interactive install libvirt-client libvirt-daemon libvirt-daemon-qemu qemu-arm qemu-tools
  elif check_network && check_command yum; then
    echo "Older Red Hat-based system detected"
    echo "Installing required system packages..."
    yum install -y python3-pip tar ipmitool perf freeipmi libgpiod-utils stress-ng kexec-tools
    yum install -y bpftrace || echo "WARNING: bpftrace unavailable; CMDQV tests will not run"
    yum install -y libvirt-client libvirt-daemon libvirt-daemon-driver-qemu qemu-kvm qemu-img
  else
    echo "WARNING: Unable to detect package manager or network unavailable."
    echo "WARNING: Manual package installation required."
    echo "Please ensure the following packages are installed on your system:"
    echo "  - python3-pip"
    echo "  - tar"
    echo "  - ipmitool"
    echo "  - perf/linux-tools"
    echo "  - freeipmi"
    echo "  - stress-ng"
    echo "  - kexec-tools"
    echo "  - bpftrace"
    echo "  - virsh/libvirt and qemu-system-aarch64 or qemu-kvm support"
    echo "  - Linux kernel headers (matching your running kernel)"
  fi

  enable_libvirt_services

  ensure_python_cmd
}

  uninstall_existing_greenlit

# Install from local wheel files
install_from_local_wheels() {
  if [ ! -d "$LOCAL_WHL_DIR" ]; then
    echo "ERROR: Wheel directory '$LOCAL_WHL_DIR' does not exist"
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "Installing from local wheels in: $LOCAL_WHL_DIR"

  # Get unique package names from wheel files into array
  mapfile -t WHL_PKGS < <(find "$LOCAL_WHL_DIR" -name "*.whl" -exec basename {} \; | cut -d'-' -f1 | sort -u)

  if [ ${#WHL_PKGS[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: No wheel files found in '$LOCAL_WHL_DIR'"
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "Installing packages: ${WHL_PKGS[*]}"

  if [[ " ${WHL_PKGS[*]} " == *" greenlit "* ]]; then
    uninstall_existing_greenlit
  fi

  # Install wheels without internet access
  if ! "${PYTHON_CMD}" -m pip install --ignore-installed --no-index --find-links "$LOCAL_WHL_DIR" "${WHL_PKGS[@]}"; then
    echo "ERROR: Local wheel installation failed"
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "Local wheel installation complete"
}

    echo "ERROR: Packaged GreenLiT runtime helper directory is missing: ${private_bin_source}"
    exit 1
  fi

  echo "Creating GreenLiT configuration directories..."
  mkdir -p "${PRIVATE_BIN_DIR}"
  mkdir -p /usr/share/greenlit/confs.d
  mkdir -p /usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir

  echo "Copying private runtime helpers..."
  cp -R "${private_bin_source}/." "${PRIVATE_BIN_DIR}/"
  find "${PRIVATE_BIN_DIR}" -type d -name __pycache__ -prune -exec rm -rf {} +
  find "${PRIVATE_BIN_DIR}" -type f -name '*.pyc' -delete

  echo "Copying configuration files..."
  cp confs/hardware-manifest.json /usr/share/greenlit/
  cp confs/glt-confs.d/* /usr/share/greenlit/confs.d/

  echo "Copying external test scripts..."
  if [ -d "external_tests" ]; then
    cp -r external_tests/* /usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir/
    # Ensure all scripts are executable
    find /usr/share/greenlit/executing_dir -type f -name "*.sh" -exec chmod +x {} \;
  fi
  write_install_config
}

  echo "Configuring systemd service for GreenLiT..."
  mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/systemd/system

  cp confs/greenlit.service /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/
  sed -i "s|/usr/bin/glt-test-suite|${SAVED_SCRIPTS:-/usr/local/bin}/glt-test-suite|" \

# Function to check Secure Boot status and warn about MOK keys
check_secure_boot() {
  local sb_enabled=false

  # Check via mokutil first
  if check_command mokutil; then
    if mokutil --sb-state 2>/dev/null | grep -q "SecureBoot enabled"; then
      sb_enabled=true
    fi
  else
    # Fallback: read EFI variable directly
    local sb_var="/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-8be4df61-93ca-11d2-aa0d-00e098032b8c"
    if [ -f "${sb_var}" ]; then
      local val
      val=$(od -An -tx1 -j4 -N1 "${sb_var}" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ')
      if [ "${val}" = "01" ]; then
        sb_enabled=true
      fi
    fi
  fi

  if [ "${sb_enabled}" = false ]; then
    return
  fi

  echo
  echo "NOTE: Secure Boot is enabled on this system."
  echo "Some GreenLiT tests build and load custom kernel modules."
  echo "These modules must be signed with a MOK key or they will be rejected."

  local mok_dir="/var/lib/shim-signed/mok"
  if [ -f "${mok_dir}/MOK.priv" ] && [ -f "${mok_dir}/MOK.der" ]; then
    echo "MOK keys found at ${mok_dir} -- module signing is ready."
  else
    echo
    echo "WARNING: No MOK keys found at ${mok_dir}."
    echo "Options:"
    echo "  1. Disable Secure Boot in UEFI/BIOS firmware settings"
    echo "  2. Set up MOK keys: see docs/user-guides/secure-boot.md"
    echo "     Quick setup on Ubuntu:"
    echo "       sudo update-secureboot-policy --new-key"
    echo "       sudo update-secureboot-policy --enroll-key"
  fi
  echo
}

}

"""
Utilities for inspecting PCI device capabilities via lspci and sysfs.
"""

import os
import re
import struct
import subprocess
from typing import Optional

from common import glt_utils

# Extended Capability names as printed by lspci.
EXT_CAP_ACS = "Access Control Services"
EXT_CAP_ATS = "Address Translation Service (ATS)"

# Known PCI vendor / device IDs.
ASPEED_VENDOR_ID = "1a03"
ASPEED_AST1150_DEVICE_ID = "1150"

# PCI class prefix for USB host controllers (UHCI/OHCI/EHCI/xHCI = 0x0c03xx).
PCI_CLASS_USB_HOST = "0x0c03"

_BDF_RE = re.compile(r"^([0-9a-fA-F]{4}:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}\.[0-9a-fA-F])\s")
_BDF_BARE_RE = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-fA-F]{4}:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}\.[0-9a-fA-F]$")

# Stricter BDF form (lowercase hex, single-digit function) for callers that
# splice untrusted input into a sysfs path and must reject path-traversal
# payloads such as "../../etc/passwd". Prefer _BDF_BARE_RE for general
# matching; use this variant when path safety matters.
BDF_STRICT_RE = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-f]{4}:[0-9a-f]{2}:[0-9a-f]{2}\.[0-7]$")


def get_bdfs_with_ext_cap(cap_name: str) -> list[str]:
    """Find all PCI devices that advertise a given extended capability.

    Runs ``lspci -Dvv`` and parses the output for capability entries
    matching *cap_name*.

    Args:
        cap_name: Capability name as printed by lspci
                  (e.g. "Access Control Services").

    Returns:
        List of domain-prefixed BDF strings (e.g. "0000:00:1f.0")
        that have the capability, or empty list on failure.
    """
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["lspci", "-Dvv"],
            capture_output=True, text=True, check=False,
        )
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return []

    if result.returncode != 0:
        return []

    matched_bdfs = []
    current_bdf = None

    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        bdf_match = _BDF_RE.match(line)
        if bdf_match:
            current_bdf = bdf_match.group(1)
            continue

        if current_bdf and cap_name in line:
            matched_bdfs.append(current_bdf)
            current_bdf = None

    return matched_bdfs


def get_bdfs_by_pci_id(vendor_id: str, device_id: Optional[str] = None) -> list[str]:
    """Find PCI devices matching a vendor (and optionally device) ID.

    Args:
        vendor_id: Four-digit hexadecimal PCI vendor ID.
        device_id: Optional four-digit hexadecimal PCI device ID. When
            omitted, all devices from the given vendor are returned.

    Returns:
        List of domain-prefixed BDF strings for matching devices, or empty
        list when lspci is unavailable, fails, or finds no matches.
    """
    pci_id = f"{vendor_id.lower()}:{device_id.lower() if device_id else ''}"
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["lspci", "-Dnn", "-d", pci_id],
            capture_output=True, text=True, check=False,
        )
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return []

    if result.returncode != 0:
        return []

    return [
        match.group(1)
        for line in result.stdout.splitlines()
        if (match := _BDF_RE.match(line))
    ]


def get_iommu_group_type(bdf: str) -> Optional[str]:
    """Return the active IOMMU domain type for ``bdf``.

    The per-group sysfs ``type`` reports the domain actually attached to the
    device, including ``identity`` for untranslated DMA and ``DMA`` or
    ``DMA-FQ`` for translated DMA.

    Returns None when the device has no IOMMU group or its group type cannot
    be read. Both cases mean callers cannot validate the active domain.
    """
    group_type_path = f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/iommu_group/type"
    try:
        return glt_utils.read_sysfs_value(group_type_path)
    except OSError:
        return None


def get_pci_children(parent_bdf: str) -> list[str]:
    """Return BDFs of PCI devices directly behind ``parent_bdf``.

    Args:
        parent_bdf: Domain-prefixed BDF of a PCI bridge.

    Returns:
        List of child BDFs, or empty list when ``parent_bdf`` is absent
        from sysfs.
    """
    parent_path = f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{parent_bdf}"
    try:
        entries = os.listdir(parent_path)
    except OSError:
        return []
    return [entry for entry in entries if _BDF_BARE_RE.match(entry)]


def get_pci_parent(
    bdf: str, sysfs_root: str = "/",
) -> tuple[Optional[str], Optional[str]]:
    """Return ``(parent_bdf, error)`` for the immediate upstream PCI bridge.

    Mirrors ``pci_upstream_bridge()`` for the topology result:
    - ``(parent, None)``: ``parent`` is the sysfs parent BDF
    - ``(None, None)``: ``bdf`` sits on a root bus (no upstream PCI bridge)
    - ``(None, reason)``: lookup failed because ``bdf`` is malformed or the
      sysfs path is missing or cannot be resolved
    """
    if not _BDF_BARE_RE.match(bdf):
        return None, f"malformed BDF {bdf!r}"
    device_link = os.path.join(
        sysfs_root, "sys", "bus", "pci", "devices", bdf,
    )
    try:
        resolved = os.path.realpath(device_link, strict=True)
    except OSError as exc:
        return None, f"cannot resolve {device_link}: {exc}"
    parent = os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(resolved))
    if not _BDF_BARE_RE.match(parent):
        return None, None
    parent_link = os.path.join(
        sysfs_root, "sys", "bus", "pci", "devices", parent,
    )
    if not os.path.exists(parent_link):
        return None, f"upstream {parent} of {bdf} is missing from sysfs"
    return parent, None


def get_reset_methods(bdf: str, sysfs_root: str = "/") -> Optional[list[str]]:
    """Return the tokens from ``reset_method``, or None if unreadable.

    An absent ``reset_method`` file means no methods are advertised and
    returns an empty list. Other OS errors return None so callers can treat
    the device as unvalidated rather than as "bus is hidden".
    """
    path = os.path.join(
        sysfs_root, "sys", "bus", "pci", "devices", bdf, "reset_method",
    )
    try:
        content = glt_utils.read_sysfs_value(path)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return []
    except OSError:
        return None
    return content.split()


def read_config_word(
    bdf: str, offset: int, sysfs_root: str = "/",
) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return a little-endian 16-bit word from PCI config space.

    Reads two bytes at ``offset`` from
    ``<sysfs_root>/sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/config``. None if ``bdf`` is
    malformed, ``offset`` is negative, or the read fails (missing device,
    permission, or short read).
    """
    if not _BDF_BARE_RE.match(bdf) or offset < 0:
        return None
    cfg_path = os.path.join(
        sysfs_root, "sys", "bus", "pci", "devices", bdf, "config",
    )
    try:
        with open(cfg_path, "rb") as cfg:
            cfg.seek(offset)
            raw_bytes = cfg.read(2)
    except OSError:
        return None
    if len(raw_bytes) < 2:
        return None
    (raw,) = struct.unpack("<H", raw_bytes)
    return raw


def get_pci_class(bdf: str) -> Optional[str]:
    """Return the PCI class for a device, as a hex string from sysfs.

    Args:
        bdf: Domain-prefixed BDF of the device.

    Returns:
        Hex string like ``"0x0c0330"`` (24 bits: class, subclass, prog-if),
        or ``None`` if the class file cannot be read.
    """
    class_file = f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/class"
    try:
        with open(class_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            return fh.read().strip()
    except OSError:
        return None


def default_route_ifaces() -> set:
    """Return the interface names holding an IPv4 or IPv6 default route.

    Reads /proc/net/route (IPv4) and /proc/net/ipv6_route (IPv6). Returns
    an empty set when the readable table(s) contain no default route.

    Raises:
        OSError: if neither route table is readable. Callers that gate
        destructive PCI operations must treat this as fail-closed — an
        empty set must not be confused with "no management NIC".
    """
    ifaces = set()
    any_readable = False
    try:
        with open("/proc/net/route", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            lines = f.readlines()
        any_readable = True
    except OSError:
        lines = []
    for line in lines[1:]:
        fields = line.split()
        if len(fields) >= 2 and fields[1] == "00000000":
            ifaces.add(fields[0])

    try:
        with open("/proc/net/ipv6_route", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            lines6 = f.readlines()
        any_readable = True
    except OSError:
        lines6 = []
    for line in lines6:
        fields = line.split()
        # All-zero destination with prefix length 00 is the IPv6 default
        # route; the interface name is the last field.
        if len(fields) >= 10 and fields[0] == "0" * 32 and fields[1] == "00":
            ifaces.add(fields[-1])

    if not any_readable:
        raise OSError(
            "neither /proc/net/route nor /proc/net/ipv6_route is readable")
    return ifaces


def _iface_pci_bdf(iface):
    """Return the PCI BDF backing a network interface, or None if not PCI."""
    # Domain-prefixed PCI BDF sysfs path component (e.g. "0000:01:00.0").
    bdf_component_re = re.compile(
        r"^[0-9a-fA-F]{4}:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}:[0-9a-fA-F]{2}\.[0-7]$")
    base = os.path.basename(
        os.path.realpath(f"/sys/class/net/{iface}/device"))
    return base if bdf_component_re.match(base) else None


def iface_pci_bdfs(iface, _seen=None) -> set:
    """Return the PCI BDF(s) of the physical NIC(s) backing `iface`.

    A directly PCI-backed interface maps to its own BDF; bond/bridge/VLAN
    interfaces are descended through /sys/class/net/<if>/lower_* links and
    bonding/slaves until PCI-backed interfaces are found.

    Args:
        iface: Network interface name (e.g. "eth0", "bond0").
        _seen: Internal recursion guard; callers must not pass it.

    Returns:
        set: Lower-cased domain-prefixed BDF strings, or an empty set if no
        physical PCI NIC backs the interface.
    """
    if _seen is None:
        _seen = set()
    if iface in _seen:
        return set()
    _seen.add(iface)

    direct = _iface_pci_bdf(iface)
    if direct is not None:
        return {direct.lower()}

    lowers = []
    try:
        entries = os.listdir(f"/sys/class/net/{iface}")
    except (FileNotFoundError, NotADirectoryError):
        entries = []
    for entry in entries:
        if entry.startswith("lower_"):
            lowers.append(entry[len("lower_"):])
    try:
        lowers.extend(glt_utils.read_sysfs_value(
            f"/sys/class/net/{iface}/bonding/slaves").split())
    except PermissionError:
        raise
    except OSError:
        pass

    bdfs = set()
    for lower in lowers:
        bdfs |= iface_pci_bdfs(lower, _seen)
    return bdfs


def is_ats_enabled(bdf: str) -> Optional[bool]:
    """Return whether ``bdf`` conclusively shows ATS enabled.

    Args:
        bdf: Domain-prefixed BDF of the device.

    Returns:
        True or False when the Address Translation Service capability block
        reports ``ATSCtl: Enable+`` or ``Enable-``. Returns None when lspci is
        unavailable, fails, or does not expose a conclusive ``ATSCtl`` value.
    """
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["lspci", "-vvv", "-s", bdf],
            capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
        )
    except (OSError, subprocess.CalledProcessError):
        return None

    in_ats_capability = False
    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        stripped = line.strip()
        if stripped.startswith("Capabilities:"):
            in_ats_capability = EXT_CAP_ATS in stripped
            continue
        if in_ats_capability and stripped.startswith("ATSCtl:"):
            if "Enable+" in stripped:
                return True
            if "Enable-" in stripped:
                return False
            return None

    return None


def mounted_block_devices() -> set:
    """Return base names of block devices backing mounted filesystems.

    Parses /proc/mounts and resolves each /dev/* mount source through
    symlinks (e.g. /dev/mapper/vg-root -> dm-0) to its kernel device name.

    Returns:
        set: Block device base names (e.g. {"nvme0n1p2", "dm-0"}), or an
        empty set when /proc/mounts is readable but has no /dev/* mounts.

    Raises:
        OSError: if /proc/mounts is unreadable. Callers that gate
        destructive PCI operations must treat this as fail-closed — an
        empty set must not be confused with "no mounted storage".
    """
    with open("/proc/mounts", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    devs = set()
    for line in lines:
        fields = line.split()
        if not fields or not fields[0].startswith("/dev/"):
            continue
        devs.add(os.path.basename(os.path.realpath(fields[0])))
    return devs


def block_device_physical_leaves(dev, _seen=None) -> set:
    """Return the physical leaf block devices backing `dev`.

    Recursively walks /sys/class/block/<dev>/slaves so stacked devices
    (LVM/dm, md RAID, dm-crypt — e.g. /dev/mapper/vg-root -> /dev/dm-0)
    resolve down to their real backing disks. A device with no slaves is
    its own leaf.

    Args:
        dev: Block device base name (e.g. "dm-0", "nvme0n1p2").
        _seen: Internal recursion guard; callers must not pass it.

    Returns:
        set: Leaf block device base names backing `dev`.
    """
    if _seen is None:
        _seen = set()
    if dev in _seen:
        return set()
    _seen.add(dev)
    try:
        slaves = os.listdir(f"/sys/class/block/{dev}/slaves")
    except (FileNotFoundError, NotADirectoryError):
        slaves = []
    if not slaves:
        return {dev}
    leaves = set()
    for slave in slaves:
        leaves |= block_device_physical_leaves(slave, _seen)
    return leaves


def _pci_path_bdfs(sysfs_path: str) -> set:
    """Collect domain-prefixed PCI BDF path components from a sysfs path."""
    return {
        part.lower()
        for part in sysfs_path.split(os.sep)
        if _BDF_BARE_RE.match(part)
    }


def unsafe_pci_bdfs() -> set:
    """BDFs that must never be unbound for destructive PCI rebinds.

    Computes:

    - For each default-route interface: the PCI BDF(s) from
      ``iface_pci_bdfs``; plus, when ``/sys/class/net/<iface>/device``
      exists, every PCI BDF component on that sysfs path (ancestors of a
      directly PCI-backed iface). Bond/bridge/VLAN tops without a
      ``device`` link contribute only the lower physical BDFs from
      ``iface_pci_bdfs`` (no ancestor walk of each slave).
    - For each mounted block device: the **leaf** PCI BDF behind the
      physical backing disk only (bridge/root-port ancestors are not
      included).

    Raises:
        OSError: if default-route tables or /proc/mounts are unreadable,
        or if sysfs resolution hits a non-absence error (e.g.
        ``PermissionError``). Callers that gate destructive PCI
        operations must treat this as fail-closed — an empty set must
        not be confused with "nothing to protect".
    """
    unsafe = set()
    for iface in default_route_ifaces():
        unsafe |= {b.lower() for b in iface_pci_bdfs(iface)}
        device_link = f"/sys/class/net/{iface}/device"
        if os.path.exists(device_link):
            unsafe |= _pci_path_bdfs(os.path.realpath(device_link))
    for dev in mounted_block_devices():
        for leaf in block_device_physical_leaves(dev):
            resolved = os.path.realpath(f"/sys/class/block/{leaf}")
            bdfs = [b.lower() for b in resolved.split(os.sep)
                    if _BDF_BARE_RE.match(b)]
            if bdfs:
                unsafe.add(bdfs[-1])
    return unsafe
def sysfs_path_to_pci_bdf(path: str) -> Optional[str]:
    """Walk a sysfs path upward and return the first valid PCI BDF segment.

    Args:
        path: A sysfs path (e.g. a resolved device symlink target).

    Returns:
        The first path segment, walking from the leaf upward, that is a
        well-formed BDF (per ``BDF_STRICT_RE``) present under
        ``/sys/bus/pci/devices``, or ``None`` if no such segment exists.
    """
    while path and path != "/":
        base = os.path.basename(path)
        if BDF_STRICT_RE.fullmatch(base) and os.path.exists(f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{base}"):
            return base
        path = os.path.dirname(path)
    return None


def bdf_in_translated_domain(bdf: str) -> bool:
    """Return whether ``bdf`` sits in a translating DMA or DMA-FQ IOMMU group.

    Args:
        bdf: Domain-prefixed BDF of the device.

    Returns:
        ``True`` when the device's ``iommu_group/type`` sysfs attribute is
        ``DMA`` or ``DMA-FQ``, ``False`` otherwise (including when ``bdf`` is
        malformed, or the device or its IOMMU group is not present).
    """
    if not BDF_STRICT_RE.fullmatch(bdf):
        return False
    group_link = f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/iommu_group"
    if not os.path.exists(group_link):
        return False
    try:
        group = os.path.realpath(group_link)
        with open(os.path.join(group, "type"), encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            group_type = handle.read().strip()
    except OSError:
        return False
    return group_type in ("DMA", "DMA-FQ")


def pci_bdfs_backing_mount(mountpoint: str = "/") -> set:
    """Return the PCI BDFs of the physical devices backing ``mountpoint``.

    Resolves the mount source through ``mounted_block_devices`` and
    ``block_device_physical_leaves``, so stacked devices (LVM/dm, MD) reduce to
    the physical disks underneath, then maps each leaf to the PCI device it
    hangs off.

    Args:
        mountpoint: Mount point to resolve, e.g. ``"/"``.

    Returns:
        set: Domain-prefixed BDFs, empty when ``mountpoint`` is not backed by a
        ``/dev/*`` source or has no PCI device beneath it. An empty set does
        not distinguish "nothing found" from "could not look"; callers gating
        destructive operations must check readability themselves rather than
        treating this as fail-closed.

    Raises:
        OSError: if /proc/mounts is unreadable.
    """
    mounted = mounted_block_devices()
    source_dev = None
    with open("/proc/mounts", "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            fields = line.split()
            if (len(fields) >= 2 and fields[1] == mountpoint
                    and fields[0].startswith("/dev/")):
                source_dev = os.path.basename(os.path.realpath(fields[0]))
                break
    if source_dev is None or source_dev not in mounted:
        return set()

    bdfs = set()
    for leaf in block_device_physical_leaves(source_dev):
        bdf = sysfs_path_to_pci_bdf(
            os.path.realpath(f"/sys/class/block/{leaf}/device")
        )
        if bdf:
            bdfs.add(bdf)
    return bdfs
